newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rubber output seen rising in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rubber output seen rising in 1997.

text.p: Sri Lanka's rubber production is expected to rise to 118 million kg this year on the back of firm prices after a 6.5 percent increase in 1996, government officials said on Tuesday.

Despite a severe drought, the island's rubber crop rose to 112.5 million kg in 1996 from 105.7 million kg in 1995, P. Liyanarachchi, director-general of the Rubber Development Department, told Reuters.

"Production rose last year because high prices helped the industry," he said. "Now producers have more confidence in rubber. They're paying more attention to maintaining their lands now that they are getting better prices."
Dr Keerthi Tillekeratne, director of the government Rubber Research Institute (RRI), said management firms running rubber estates had improved productivity after getting a longer lease on the land.
"The management companies are doing a better job," Tillekeratne said.

"Also the use of rain guards has shown a clear improvement. High-yielding clones are also coming into bearing, while subsidy payments to small cultivators, who produce the bulk of the crop, are being done very effectively," he added.
Sri Lanka produces just two percent of the world natural rubber output, having slipped from the world's fourth-biggest rubber producer to eighth in 25 years.
Rubber production is forecast to rise to 126 million kg by 2000, Tillekeratne said. Production was a record 155 million kg in 1978.
Liyanarachchi said rubber prices were expected to remain firm this year after soaring to record highs over the past two years.
"Prices are unlikely to drop. Natural rubber has a better demand now, with Western markets being more concerned about the environmental effects of using synthetic rubber," he said.
